strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated architectural decoupling of scene representation (viewpoint tokens) from input images, addressing a real scalability bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction methods that rely on full multi-view attention.

The two-stage attention scheme (per-view cross-attention + viewpoint self-attention) is a sensible and effective way to reduce quadratic complexity while retaining global multi-view consistency, and the FLOPs/memory/time analysis (Tab. 6, Appendix F) substantiates the claimed efficiency gains.

Extensive experiments across RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID (cross-dataset generalization), with multiple viewpoint/resolution configurations, consistently show state-of-the-art or near-SOTA PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS while using substantially fewer Gaussians and less compute/memory than strong baselines (GS-LRM, DepthSplat, MVSplat, pixelSplat, LongLRM).

Thorough ablation studies (number of layers, iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention necessity, group-attention alternative, initialization schemes) support the individual design choices rather than just the overall pipeline.

The wide-coverage comparison against optimization-based methods (3D-GS, Mip-Splatting) and LongLRM, including a fine-tuning variant, is a nice demonstration that feed-forward reconstruction can approach or exceed per-scene optimization quality at a fraction of the time.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and provides substantial supplementary detail (implementation, additional ablations, qualitative figures) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'iterative refinement' framing as analogous to gradient-based optimization is more a conceptual/motivational narrative than a rigorously established equivalence; the ablation (single cross-attention layer + many self-attention layers) shows that repeated cross-attention helps, but doesn't strongly validate the optimizer analogy itself, which is largely rhetorical.

Self-attention across all viewpoint tokens is still, by the authors' own admission in Limitations, a bottleneck that will not scale indefinitely with view count; the largest demonstrated view count (32) is still moderate for 'wide-coverage' scenes, and no truly large-N (e.g., 100+) scaling experiment is shown beyond the DL3DV 12-view OOM comparison against DepthSplat.

The comparisons against GS-LRM and some other baselines are asterisked as reproduced without official code/pretrained models (Table 1), leaving some reliance on numbers copied from other papers rather than direct reproduction, which slightly weakens the rigor of comparison.

The method still fundamentally requires known/accurate camera poses (acknowledged as a limitation), restricting applicability relative to recent pose-free feed-forward approaches, and no experiments address this limitation empirically.

Some design choices (e.g., patch size, k=2 expansion factor for uplifting, choice of mini-batch cross-attention variant used for main results vs. MC variants) are set empirically without deeper justification or sensitivity analysis beyond a few ablation tables.

The paper does not report variance/multiple seeds or statistical significance for the reported metrics, which is common in this literature but limits certainty about the size of the sometimes small quality gaps (e.g., LPIPS differences of 0.01-0.02) relative to strongest baselines in some settings.

strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated iterative refinement framework for feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction, drawing an intuitive analogy to per-scene optimization (rendering-and-update loop) that is largely absent in prior one-shot feed-forward LRM-style methods.

The core architectural idea of decoupling the 3D representation (viewpoint embeddings) from the input image resolution is effective and addresses a genuine and well-documented problem (redundant pixel-aligned Gaussians growing with resolution/#views).

The two-stage attention scheme (per-view cross-attention + low-resolution self-attention) is a sensible and effective way to reduce the quadratic cost of full multi-view attention, and the paper provides clear FLOPs/time/memory comparisons that substantiate the efficiency claims (Tables 3, 4, 6, and Appendix F).

Extensive empirical evaluation across RE10K, DL3DV, and ACID, with multiple viewpoint/resolution configurations, cross-dataset generalization, wide-baseline settings, and comparisons against both feed-forward (pixelSplat, MVSplat, GS-LRM, DepthSplat, Gen-Den, LongLRM) and optimization-based (3D-GS, Mip-Splatting) baselines. Results consistently show favorable PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS with substantially fewer Gaussians and much lower inference time/memory.

Thorough ablation studies (number of layers, iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention removal, group-attention, initialization strategies) that isolate the contribution of each design component and largely support the paper's claims.

The token uplifting mechanism to bridge the resolution mismatch between low-res viewpoint queries and high-res image keys/values is a reasonable technical contribution beyond simple downsampling-based cross-attention.

Good scalability demonstration: the method handles more input views (8, 12, 16, 24, 32) with sub-linear cost growth and outperforms DepthSplat, which runs out of memory in the high-resolution multi-view setting.
weaknesses: Novelty concerns: the two-stage cross/self-attention design (decoupled query tokens interacting with per-view features, then globally aggregated) closely resembles ideas from perceiver-style architectures and is also reminiscent of alternating-attention designs (e.g., VGGT, cited in the appendix) and iterative slot/query-based reconstruction. The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of how it differs conceptually from these related iterative-query architectures beyond the specific 3D-GS decoding.

The 'iterative refinement' framing as analogous to per-scene gradient-based optimization is more a conceptual motivation/narrative than a rigorously established mechanism—there's no explicit loss-based feedback signal at each layer (e.g., no rendering-and-residual computation at intermediate layers), so the claimed analogy to actual optimization (gradient descent) is somewhat loose; the ablation for 'iterative refinement' just tests where cross-attention is placed, not whether real feedback/error signals drive refinement.

GS-LRM, one of the strongest baselines, is marked with '*' because official code/pretrained model are unavailable, and only single-number results from the paper are copied into Table 1; no results for GS-LRM appear in later, more comprehensive tables (DL3DV, cross-dataset, wide-coverage), limiting a full head-to-head comparison against a key competitor.

The number of unique target views and camera-overlap definitions across different tables (varying viewpoint/resolution notations (V, H/F, F)) can be difficult to parse in detail; more consolidated protocol descriptions and fewer bespoke naming conventions would improve clarity and reproducibility for readers trying to replicate exact settings.

Some inference-time/memory-comparisons mix hardware (RTX 4090, H100, A100) across different tables (e.g., DepthSplat evaluated on H100 due to OOM on 4090 in Table 4, while Ours run on 4090), which, though explained, complicates strictly apples-to-apples comparisons of wall-clock efficiency claims.

The paper still depends on known camera poses (typically from COLMAP), and while this is acknowledged as a limitation, it somewhat limits real-world applicability compared to emerging pose-free feed-forward reconstruction methods; no experiments address robustness under noisy/estimated poses.

The self-attention module, which enables cross-view global consistency, still scales quadratically with the number of viewpoints (acknowledged in Limitations); given the paper's polish around scalability, this residual bottleneck is not empirically stress-tested at very large view counts (e.g., >32) to see where it breaks down.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: scalability of feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction models with respect to number of views and image resolution.

The core idea of decoupling the Gaussian/scene representation from input image resolution via compact viewpoint tokens, combined with a two-stage (cross-attention then self-attention) interaction scheme, is a sensible and reasonably novel architectural contribution that meaningfully reduces the quadratic attention cost of prior full-attention approaches (e.g., GS-LRM).

Extensive and fairly rigorous experimental evaluation: results on RE10K, DL3DV (multiple resolutions/view counts), cross-dataset generalization to ACID, wide-baseline/zero-shot tests on Tanks&Temples and Mip-NeRF360, depth/geometry evaluation against pseudo-depth and point clouds, robustness to pose noise, and post-prediction optimization comparisons.

Thorough ablation studies (model depth, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, mini-batch cross-attention variants, initialization strategies, group- vs per-view attention) that support the design choices individually.

Strong reported efficiency-quality trade-off: fewer parameters and Gaussians than baselines while achieving competitive or superior PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, notably faster inference (0.5s vs ~8min for optimization-based 3D-GS) and better scaling to more views/higher resolution than DepthSplat/Long-LRM.

The attention visualization (Fig. 8/18) provides some interpretability into the claimed 'iterative refinement' behavior, showing attended tokens converging to geometrically consistent regions across layers.
Good reproducibility support: detailed architectural and training hyperparameters, FLOPs analysis, and supplementary implementation details are provided.
weaknesses: The individual architectural components (Perceiver-style cross-attention/self-attention decomposition, mini-batch/token-subsampling for attention, Plücker ray embeddings, iterative refinement framing) are each adapted from existing works (Perceiver, VGGT's alternating attention, prior LRM works); the novelty lies primarily in combining these ideas for 3D Gaussian reconstruction rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism, which somewhat limits originality.

The 'iterative refinement as optimization' framing (analogy to gradient descent) is more of a conceptual narrative than a formally justified claim; no explicit loss/energy function is optimized at each layer, so the analogy, while illustrative, is not rigorously established.

Baseline comparisons, while broad, are largely against a limited set of recent feed-forward methods (MVSplat, DepthSplat, Gen-Den, Long-LRM); some very recent strong pixel-aligned or pose-free baselines (e.g., VGGT-based reconstruction methods) are only cited but not directly compared quantitatively.

The paper acknowledges reliance on accurate camera poses as a limitation, and the self-attention bottleneck across viewpoint tokens remains a scalability concern for very large numbers of views (e.g., Table 15 still shows non-trivial runtime growth, though no OOM).

Some ablations (e.g., Table 9's random/group-attention/init variants) are run only under a single, relatively small configuration (4 views, half resolution), which may not fully generalize to the paper's headline high-resolution/wide-coverage settings.

The quantitative gains over the strongest baseline (DepthSplat) on RE10K/DL3DV are sometimes modest (e.g., PSNR differences within ~1 dB in several settings), and improvements partly stem from using more input views or additional held-out supervision setups, which somewhat complicates head-to-head comparison fairness across differing view counts.

Presentation clarity could be improved in places: the interpretation section's gradient-descent notation is dense and not fully self-contained, and some table settings (e.g., MC variants, H/F/Q resolution codes) require cross-referencing multiple sections to parse.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically important problem: the quadratic scaling of full multi-view attention in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction models, which limits the number of input views and resolution that can be processed.

The proposed decoupling of a compact, viewpoint-centric token representation from high-resolution image tokens, combined with a two-stage cross-/self-attention scheme, is a reasonable and clearly explained engineering solution to reduce compute while retaining access to high-resolution visual cues.

The experimental section is unusually extensive for a conference paper: results are reported on RE10K, DL3DV (multiple resolutions and view-count settings), ACID (cross-dataset generalization), Tanks&Temples and Mip-NeRF360 (zero-shot), plus depth/pointmap geometry evaluation, robustness to pose noise, and detailed ablations on model size, architecture components, and FLOPs/memory/time.

The method demonstrates favorable speed/memory/#Gaussian trade-offs relative to DepthSplat, MVSplat, and Long-LRM, particularly in wide-baseline, many-view settings (e.g., completing in under 1s where Long-LRM runs out of memory at 256 views).

The attention visualization (Fig. 8/18) provides some interpretability evidence that the iterative refinement progressively attends to geometrically consistent regions across layers, supporting the core design motivation.

Ablations (Tabs. 6, 7, 9) are reasonably thorough and isolate the contributions of iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, and self-attention, strengthening the internal validity of the architectural claims.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is incremental: decoupled cross-/self-attention between compact latent tokens and image tokens is a well-established pattern (Perceiver-style architectures, Quark, LRM-type decoupling already cited by the authors), and 'iterative refinement across layers' is essentially a relabeling of a deep stack of alternating cross-/self-attention blocks (standard in many transformer-based reconstruction and VGGT-style models) rather than a fundamentally new refinement mechanism with explicit error feedback (no residual/error signal is computed and fed back; it is a forward pass through stacked blocks with weight-sharing removed per layer).

Quantitative gains over the strongest baselines are often modest (e.g., 29.24 vs 28.90/28.78 PSNR on RE10K for DepthSplat/Gen-Den; DL3DV PSNR gaps are frequently <1 dB), making it unclear whether improvements are attributable to the proposed architecture versus differences in training schedule, batch size, or parameter count, especially since GS-LRM (closed-source) is only compared on RE10K and not on the larger DL3DV/wide-baseline settings.

The method's efficiency advantage is partly a consequence of producing fewer Gaussians (resolution-decoupled low-res viewpoint tokens) rather than a purely algorithmic attention-efficiency gain; Table 17's 'same number of Gaussians' comparison, while included, only partially isolates this confound and is limited to RE10K.

The approach assumes known, accurate camera poses, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation; this restricts applicability relative to recent pose-free/pose-robust generalizable 3DGS methods (PF3plat, SelfSplat, cited by the authors) that address a harder and increasingly relevant setting.

Geometric accuracy is evaluated only indirectly via pseudo-depth from a monocular depth estimator (MoGe-2) as a proxy rather than against true ground-truth depth/point clouds in the main comparisons, and the paper itself notes recovered geometry may be less accurate than explicit geometry-supervised methods, somewhat undercutting the 'high-fidelity 3D reconstruction' framing.

No mention of code or model release, and several implementation choices (e.g., mini-batch cross-attention sampling strategy selection, token-uplifting factor k=2) appear to be heuristically tuned without principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond a single ablation setting, raising mild reproducibility concerns.

The paper's framing contrasts itself with G3R/Gen-Den as lacking 'true' iterative refinement because they do not use rendering gradients, but it does not provide a direct head-to-head ablation isolating the benefit of gradient-free forward refinement versus a simple deeper/wider non-iterative baseline with matched parameter count beyond Table 6, limiting the strength of the central claim that feedback-driven refinement per se (rather than simply more layers of cross-attention with image tokens) is responsible for the gains.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated architectural idea: decoupling the 3D Gaussian representation (viewpoint-centric embeddings) from the input image resolution, combined with an iterative, feedback-driven refinement scheme reminiscent of optimization-based 3D-GS, is a sensible and reasonably novel way to address the scalability bottleneck of pixel-aligned feed-forward Gaussian methods.

The two-stage (cross-attention then self-attention) interaction scheme and the mini-batch cross-attention variants (quarter/random-quarter) are a practical and clearly explained solution to reduce the quadratic cost of full attention across multi-view tokens, with an explicit FLOPs/time analysis (Tables 8, and supplementary Sec. E) supporting the claimed efficiency gains.

Extensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (RE10K, DL3DV at several resolutions/baselines, cross-dataset generalization to ACID, zero-shot wide-baseline DL3DV/Tanks&Temples/Mip-NeRF360) and multiple axes (view count, resolution, number of Gaussians, inference time, memory) gives a fairly comprehensive picture of when/why the method helps, including favorable comparisons to strong recent baselines (MVSplat, DepthSplat, GS-LRM, Gen-Den, Long-LRM, 3D-GS).

Thorough ablation studies (model depth/size, iterative refinement vs. single-shot, resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention vs. group-attention, initialization strategies) support most of the individual design choices rather than only reporting an end-to-end number.

Additional analyses beyond RGB PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS — geometry/depth evaluation against pseudo-depth and point clouds (NRGBD, ETH3D, TNT, Mip-NeRF360), post-prediction optimization convergence, robustness to pose noise, and attention visualizations showing progressively more accurate cross-view correspondence — substantially strengthen the evidence that the iterative refinement is doing something meaningful rather than just adding parameters.

Compact representation (fewer Gaussians for comparable/better quality) and strong scalability to large numbers of high-resolution views (e.g., 256 views without OOM, versus Long-LRM running out of memory) are practically valuable properties for real-world deployment.
weaknesses: The core techniques (cross-attention/self-attention alternation resembling Perceiver-style architectures, iterative token refinement, mini-batch/subsampled attention) are each individually well established in prior literature (Perceiver, VGGT's alternating attention, Quark, LRM/GS-LRM lineage); the paper's contribution is largely a careful combination and scaling of these ideas for 3D Gaussian reconstruction rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which somewhat limits the conceptual novelty.

The claimed 'feedback-driven' / gradient-descent interpretation (Sec. 3.2 'Interpretation' paragraph) is presented as an analogy without rigorous justification; the connection V^(l) ≈ V^(l-1) - eta*grad E is asserted rather than derived or empirically verified (e.g., no evidence that the learned updates actually behave like descent steps on a well-defined objective), so this framing risks overstating the theoretical grounding.

Structured mini-batch cross-attention variants (quarter cross-attention, random-quarter) are proposed in Fig. 4, but the main results tables mostly report only the quarter-attention (MC) variant; a clearer, consolidated comparison of all four schemes (full/half/quarter/random-quarter) on accuracy-vs-efficiency trade-offs is scattered across the supplement rather than centrally presented, making it harder to assess which sampling strategy is actually best justified.

The self-attention bottleneck across many viewpoint tokens is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but is not empirically stress-tested at very large numbers of views (e.g., beyond 256) to show where the method eventually breaks down; the presented scalability claims, while good, stop short of characterizing the actual failure point.

Reliance on accurate camera poses is acknowledged as a limitation, and while pose-noise robustness is tested (Table 14), the method is not evaluated in a pose-free or jointly-optimized-pose setting, leaving the practical applicability to real, noisy SfM pipelines only partially addressed.

Some presentation issues: dense notation and multiple viewpoint-setting abbreviations (V,H/F,F) require careful cross-referencing across tables and text, and a few qualitative results (e.g., Fig. 7, 15, 16) show visible artifacts/blur in ours vs. baselines that are not fully discussed in the main text, slightly limiting transparency about failure cases.
